content:
Google has documented what it describes as the first observed case of a cyberattack carried out end to end by artificial intelligence, with no human involved at any stage. The finding, published on November 16 by the Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant in their AI Threat Tracker report, is titled "Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold" — and the researchers leave little doubt about why they chose those words.

"For the first time," the report said, its researchers observed threat actors "using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop." Until now, AI in cyberattacks has mostly meant a human operator using a chatbot to write a phishing email or debug a piece of malware. This is different: a system that finds the flaw, builds the weapon and fires it by itself.

The discovery began with a server that should never have been visible. Google's researchers found a multi-agent framework they dubbed "exploit_agent" sitting on an exposed staging server, connected to several locally hosted large language models. Its method is as simple as it is unsettling. The framework compares the code of popular web applications before and after a vendor publishes a security patch, works out what the fix reveals about the underlying flaw, drafts a working exploit from that difference and then runs it — all without a person at the keyboard.

The server held more than the framework itself. Alongside data taken from victims, it contained scripts for internal reconnaissance, password brute-forcing and installing webshells — the hidden backdoors attackers plant to keep access to a compromised machine. It even held a script for deleting other attackers' webshells, a sign that the operator was competing for control of the same machines. Victim telemetry suggested the operator was focused on French websites in the media, entertainment and education sectors.

Google did not name a group or a state behind the framework. But [CyberScoop reported](https://www.cyberscoop.com/) that the attribution rests partly on Russian-language comments in the operation's code, including a configuration file that told its user to enter API keys for "auto-exploitation" in the file itself rather than in a chat window. Politico Europe, which reported the finding first, described the operators as Russian speakers.

The report is not about one tool. Google said adversaries are now deploying a whole family of open-source, multi-agent penetration testing frameworks — ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI — and that it has seen experimentation with another, HexStrike AI. CAIRN, which runs specialised agents through an observe, orient, decide, act loop, was used in intrusions against targets that included the aerospace sector in the United States. A custom platform built on PentAGI scanned a wide range of organisations across Asia between late August and early October 2026. And ARTEX, an autonomous penetration testing framework that was pulled from GitHub in October, had already been tied by security researchers to automated attacks on banks in Southeast Asia.

The numbers in the report show a threat that is accelerating. Google said overall vulnerability disclosures and exploits nearly doubled between January and August 2026. Zero-day exploits — flaws vendors do not know about yet — edged up from a 2025 average of eight a month to 11 a month in 2026, then jumped to 22 in August alone.

One case study shows how fast the window between disclosure and attack has become. The report traced the PaperCut print server flaws CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078, which chain together into unauthenticated remote code execution. According to GreyNoise, a campaign began four days after disclosure, reached hundreds of organisations and expanded an initial foothold to full domain administrator control within minutes. After two PHP flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, were patched on October 21, hundreds of claimed proofs of concept appeared within days. Google said most were non-functional and probably generated with large language models, leaving defenders to verify or debunk them one by one.

The report also describes a parallel economy built on stolen AI capacity. In what Google calls LLMJacking, criminals break into a company's cloud environment and spend its AI quota. In some cases single-day fraudulent charges passed $100,000, and the worst cases reached $1 million in cumulative abuse before the theft was caught. The stolen access is resold through what Google calls LLM Mixers, underground storefronts that pool stolen credentials and compute. Advertised prices ranged from $0.10 to $25 per million tokens, and one vendor, APIMart, charged five times more once a prompt passed 100,000 tokens.

The same report covers the use of AI in espionage and influence work. A suspected North Korean cluster that Google calls MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE built fake recruiter profiles whose images carried Google's SynthID watermark, then steered targets to ClickFix lures. Google said the group abused AI tools as a supply chain entry point against cryptocurrency firms in North America and Europe. State-linked and commercial influence operators, meanwhile, used large language models to produce synthetic media at scale, build localised personas and distribute political content across platforms — including one platform built on Google's own Gemini API that automated persona creation, media generation and distribution for campaigns aimed mainly at Europe and the Middle East.

Google's advice to defenders is blunt. Its SecOps team has released behaviour-based detection rules for ARTEX, and Mandiant's guidance is a five-layer defence: lock down administrative systems, use short-lived credentials, limit access, split networks, and watch for sudden spikes in API and identity activity. For organisations using AI services, the report recommends budget alerts, scanning code for leaked keys and treating any unexpected AI service activation as a warning sign.

There is, for now, one consolation. The report notes the trade-off attackers are making: these frameworks are noisy, leave known names and clear code traces, and buy speed at the cost of stealth. But Google said it expects less human involvement and better stealth as the frameworks mature, which is why the report frames the current stage as a threshold rather than a peak. [According to Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/technology/artificial-intelligence/google-flags-first-autonomous-ai-cyberattack-warns-of-growing-threats-126111700791_1.html), Google's analysts forecast that simple attacks carried out by multiple AI agents with almost no human involvement could emerge within three months, and sophisticated fully autonomous attacks within six.

Pressure is already building outside the report. California this week sued OpenAI over at least 80 AI-agent incidents, and Washington began requiring licences to ship top AI chips to five countries. John Hultquist, chief analyst at the Google Threat Intelligence Group, put the shift in plain terms: attackers using AI, he said, "don't need zero-days" any more — they need speed and scale, and the machines are now supplying both. For defenders, the lesson of the exploit_agent discovery is that the window between a patch being published and an attack arriving is no longer measured in days. It is measured in minutes, and soon it may not involve a human at all.

The scale of the change is underlined by a second, quieter trend in the same report: the tooling is cheap, open source and getting faster. That combination — free frameworks, stolen compute and machine-speed exploitation — is what makes this threshold different from every AI warning that came before it. Google's researchers spent two years predicting that artificial intelligence would eventually run a hacking campaign from end to end. On November 16, they said, they watched it happen. The question now is how quickly the rest of the industry catches up — because the attackers, by Google's own account, already have.
summary: Google's threat researchers say they have observed attackers using an AI framework to discover vulnerabilities and run exploits entirely on its own — a threshold the security industry has warned about for two years.
title: Google says AI has carried out its first fully autonomous cyberattack — with no human in the loop
